name: Butea superba

lead: Butea superba is a climbing shrub of the legume family native to India and mainland Southeast Asia. Its tuberous root is used in Thai traditional medicine as a rejuvenating and sexual tonic, and it is sold as a supplement under the name red Kwao Krua. Forum users who take it generally want hormone, libido or energy support that could carry into training, recovery and physique.

Research consists mainly of rat and cell studies, plus a small 2003 Thai randomized trial in men with erectile dysfunction. Rodent work has reported increased erectile pressure and, in one study, higher serum testosterone, while other animal data report hormonal changes at high doses.

paras: It is sold as root powder, capsules and extracts, and discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation as an add-on to other supplements. Reports on those forums mention checking bloodwork and compare it with other herbs such as tribulus; product quality and plant part vary widely between sellers.

Safety data are thin. A 2008 rat study cited by Wikipedia reported effects on blood parameters and lowered testosterone at high doses of dried material. Because it contains phytoestrogen-type isoflavones such as daidzein and genistein, effects on hormones are an area of discussion. People with medical conditions or on medication commonly consult a clinician.

angle.text: Users take it hoping for androgen and libido support that translates into better training and body composition. Human evidence concerns erectile function rather than muscle or appearance outcomes.

lead: Butea superba is a vining shrub in the legume family native to India and mainland Southeast Asia, whose tuberous roots are used in Thai traditional medicine as a rejuvenating and aphrodisiac tonic [1][2]. It is sold as red Kwao Krua, distinguished from white (Pueraria mirifica) and black (Mucuna collettii) Kwao Krua plants [3].

Its relevance to appearance is through the goals of those who take it: improved libido, energy and androgen status, which proponents link to motivation to train, recovery and body composition. Forum discussion appears on looksmax.org and in T Nation threads about naturally raising testosterone [4].

Research includes a 3-month randomized double-blind Thai trial reporting improvement in erectile function scores [5], several rat studies on erection pressure [6][7], and a rat study reporting increased serum testosterone and cognitive protection [8]. Reviews describe the human trials as small and not robust [9].

paras: Wikipedia describes B. superba as a vining shrub of the Fabaceae family; locals consider it an aphrodisiac among other effects [1]. Thai literature classes it among rejuvenating and neurotonic remedies, and one screening study examined Thai rejuvenating plants for acetylcholinesterase inhibition [10]. The tuberous roots contain flavonoids, flavonoid glycosides and sterols such as beta-sitosterol, campesterol and stigmasterol [1]; later work isolated daidzein and genistein and examined their effects on the male mouse reproductive system [11].

Threads on looksmax.org discuss starting a Butea superba course and ask what is known about it [12][13]. T Nation threads mention it among herbal options for testosterone and sex drive, alongside discussion of bloodwork and estrogen [4]. Users report varied experiences, and the community discussion is anecdotal.

The Wikipedia entry cites a 2008 rat study in which high doses of dried plant material (200 mg/kg) affected several blood parameters and lowered testosterone [1]. A separate rat study reported raised serum testosterone after two weeks at a comparable dose of extract, showing that animal findings differ between studies and preparations [8]. A cell study compared the proliferative effects of the three Kwao Krua plants on MCF-7 breast cancer cells [3]. Standardized human safety data are limited to a 3-month trial that found no apparent change in blood chemistry [5].

A 3-month randomized double-blind trial in Thai men aged roughly 30 to 70 with erectile dysfunction used a crude tuber preparation; it reported significant improvement in 4 of 5 IIEF-5 domains and noticeable improvement in 82.4 percent of patients, with no apparent change in blood tests [5]. A 2011 review of herbal erectile dysfunction treatments found B. superba among the few herbs with human studies but described those trials as not robust [9]. Wikipedia states that no placebo-controlled studies support aphrodisiac activity and that open trials gave conflicting conclusions [1]. No human trial has examined muscle, body composition or appearance outcomes.
Animal studies include increased intracavernous pressure in aged rats [6] and in diabetic rats [7], and cognitive protection plus raised serum testosterone in aged male rats [8].
